pa_philly.blurb: Climbing in Philadelphia is almost entirely bouldering, tucked into the city's creekside parks and centred on Wissahickon Valley Park, where the rock is Wissahickon schist and the wooded valley feels far more remote than the surroundings suggest. Problems start at the easiest V grades and reach into the V9 range, with the bulk in the easy to middle grades. A small amount of roped climbing sits alongside: a few top-rope, sport and trad lines from about 5.7 to 5.12, mostly on Livezey Rock, a south-facing schist wall that stays shaded by trees in the morning and takes sun through much of the rest of the day. Pennypack Park and Cobbs Creek hold smaller groups of boulders.

tn_tennessee_wall_the.blurb: A long line of hard sandstone in the Tennessee River Gorge, a short drive northwest of Chattanooga. This is a trad crag first: mostly single-pitch lines, a handful of multipitch routes in the western section, and a few sport climbs. Grades run from about 5.6 to 5.13, with the heart of the range at 5.10 and 5.11 and a decent spread of 5.8 and 5.9 for newer leaders. Protection is usually plentiful, so a standard rack of nuts and cams does the job. The wall faces south and takes sun all day, which makes it a prime winter destination and a poor choice for summer heat; September through June is the good stretch. Orange Blossom Wall is the largest section, followed by Paradise Wall, The Wasteland and The Amphitheater.

ca_central_gorge.blurb: Central Gorge is the busiest stretch of Owens River Gorge, a canyon the river carved through volcanic welded tuff near Bishop on the eastern edge of the Sierra Nevada. Nearly everything here is sport climbing, with a small amount of trad. Walls sit close together, so a day can hold a great many pitches, and the popular ones are often crowded. Grades centre on 5.10 and 5.11, with a solid helping of 5.9 and easier and a short tail up into 5.13. Expect edges, pockets and cracks on mostly near-vertical rock. The gorge climbs through the year, though summer can be hot. Great Wall of China, Soul Power Wall, Faulty Tower and Banana Belt are among the largest crags.

nh_black_jack_boulders.blurb: Rumney is best known for sport cliffs, but its bouldering is excellent too, and Black Jack Boulders is the main bouldering zone: boulders scattered among trees and cliffs and split into many small sub-areas such as Upper Black Jacks, Western Black Jacks, the Zig Zag Area and the Entrance Boulders. Nearly everything is a boulder problem, with a handful of crack lines on trad or top rope. The grade range is wide, from V0 up past V10, with a steady supply of problems from V0 through V8 and a thin tail of very hard ones. Styles vary from cracks and dynos to face climbing, pockets, arêtes and roofs, and there is still room for new problems.

pa_central_pa.blurb: Central Pennsylvania centres on the area around State College, and bouldering makes up most of it, from the easiest V grades to V12, with the weight in the V0 to V4 range. Hunter's Rocks is the big one: a sandstone boulder field on a mountaintop about 25 miles south of State College, where the boulders poke above the trees and the friction is praised. The rock is described regionally as grippy and full of features, steep to vertical and sometimes overhanging. Donation Rocks adds a mix of top-rope, sport and trad, and roped climbs overall run from about 5.4 to 5.12. Rock Run and Blue Run Rocks round out the larger zones, and there is a little ice as well.

co_elevenmile_canyon.blurb: A granite canyon on the South Platte River about an hour west of Colorado Springs, with crags strung along a nine-mile road that follows the water up to a reservoir dam. Sport climbing leads, trad is close behind, and there is some bouldering. Many of the domes, such as Elevenmile Dome, Arch Rock, Turret Dome and Pine Cone Dome, hold plenty of moderate multipitch and single-pitch lines, with newer low-angle sport routes among them. Harder sport and trad in the 5.11 to 5.13 range sits on the steeper walls. Overall grades run from about 5.4 to 5.14, centred on 5.7 to 5.12. At roughly 8,200 feet the season is shorter and cooler than most Front Range crags, and shady walls suit the summer.
